title: Why I Founded CatchDog
excerpt: CatchDog started as a workflow automation idea. But building a company with generative AI at its core quickly changed the scope of what was possible.
body:
When I started building CatchDog LLC, the initial idea was very specific: help small and mid-sized businesses automate workflows and connect the tools they already use.

But something became clear very quickly. A company born with generative AI at its core does not remain limited to one category of service. As the technology evolves, the scope of what can be built also expands.

That is why CatchDog LLC gradually became more than a workflow automation project. Today, the work can include functional systems, lightweight interfaces, dashboards, SaaS-style prototypes, operational automations, audiovisual content, explainers, and AI-assisted problem solving. Not because the goal is to “do everything,” but because many business problems do not fit neatly into one technical box.

Most SMBs do not need a massive software implementation. They need someone who can understand the problem, translate it into a practical digital solution, and deliver something usable without turning the process into a long and expensive enterprise project.

This is the logic behind CatchDog LLC: use AI not as a gimmick, but as a working layer that helps move faster across strategy, systems, interfaces, content, and execution.

I do not think clients always need to know every tool or technical step behind the solution. What they need is clarity, functionality, and results they can actually use.

That is the kind of company I wanted to build: small, flexible, AI-native, and focused on solving real operational problems with lightweight technology.

title: The Operating Nervous System: How AI Agents Are Rewiring Business Operations
excerpt: Organizations are hitting the same wall: fragmented tools, repetitive tasks, and communication flows that nobody designed — they just accumulated.
body:
CatchDog was born from a simple premise: most small and mid-sized businesses do not need heavy enterprise software. They need practical digital systems that solve real operational problems. At first, that meant workflow automation and tool integration. But a company built natively with generative AI does not stay confined to one narrow category. As the technology evolves, so does the range of problems it can address.

That is why CatchDog is not just an “automation company.” It builds end-to-end functional systems, interfaces, control panels, lightweight dashboards, SaaS-style prototypes, audiovisual assets, scripts, explainers, and AI-assisted operational solutions. The client does not need to know every tool, API, model, platform, or technical layer behind the result. What matters is that the problem is understood, translated into a usable system, and delivered in a way the business can actually operate.

This is the real shift: generative AI allows a small, flexible team to cover areas that used to require separate specialists, agencies, developers, designers, content producers, and consultants. CatchDog can move from diagnosing a workflow problem to building a prototype, creating a front-end interface, designing supporting content, and automating repetitive tasks. It is not “doing everything” in the abstract. It is doing almost everything a business needs in the space of lightweight, functional technology.

For SMBs, this matters because speed, clarity, and usefulness are often more valuable than complexity. CatchDog turns messy operational needs into systems, assets, and workflows that reduce friction and accelerate execution. It is a company designed for the AI era: not defined by one service category, but by the ability to keep adapting as the tools expand and the business problems become clearer.

title: You don't need to deal with technology
excerpt: Most companies don’t have an AI problem. They have operational friction: disconnected tools, manual steps, and systems that don’t work together. The worst outcome is using AI where human judgment is essential, while people keep wasting time on low-value repetitive tasks.
body:
Most businesses don’t wake up thinking they need AI.

They struggle with something much more concrete: too many tools, too many manual steps, too much time lost moving information from one place to another.

The problem is rarely “we need artificial intelligence.”

The problem is usually: this process is slow, this follow-up depends on memory, this information is duplicated, this tool does not talk to that tool, this client experience feels messy, this team is wasting time on work that should not require human attention.

That distinction matters.

Because the point is not to add AI everywhere. In fact, one of the worst mistakes a business can make is using AI where human judgment, trust, taste, or strategic thinking are essential.

The real opportunity is different: use technology to remove the operational weight that keeps people away from the work where they actually create value.

Most companies already have enough tools. Email, spreadsheets, forms, CRMs, calendars, cloud folders, messaging apps. What they usually lack is coherence.

When systems don’t communicate, people become the interface.

They copy, paste, check, remind, update, resend, rename, classify, chase, and follow up. That is where time is lost. That is where errors appear. That is where good teams become tired teams.

This is where AI can matter — not as a product label, but as part of a practical system.

A useful system can classify information, prioritize requests, trigger the right follow-up, route a lead, organize documents, draft a first response, or connect different tools into one operational flow.

The client does not need to deal with the technology behind it.

The client needs to explain the business problem clearly.

That is the kind of work I want to do with CatchDog: sit with a business owner, understand where the friction is, and build lightweight systems that make the operation easier, faster, and more coherent.

I have been working with AI as a collaborative layer since 2018, starting with research at AI Lab, University of Buenos Aires. Not as a tool to “prompt,” but as a way to extend thinking and build systems around it.

That is the foundation behind CatchDog LLC.

Most of the time, clients don’t ask for AI.

They ask for things to work.

And that is exactly the point.

title: From Tech Analysis to Building With AI
excerpt: For years, I studied, reported on, and explained technology. Generative AI changed something deeper: it gave people with strategic, humanistic, and analytical backgrounds the ability to build, not just interpret.
body:
For years, my work was to observe technology, understand it, explain it, and translate its impact for broader audiences.

As a journalist, I covered software, AI, Web3, startups, business models, and the way technology was reshaping economies in Latin America and the United States. I was not only reporting on tools or companies. I was trying to understand the social transformation behind them.

Artificial intelligence always felt different to me. Unlike other innovations that affect specific sectors, AI was clearly going to change the way society thinks, works, communicates, decides, and creates. That is why I followed it closely, both as a journalist and through academic and research work.

At the same time, since 2010, I have also built and led agencies in digital marketing and public relations. I wrote, designed strategies, advised clients, analyzed business models, and worked closely with technological change. In many ways, I became a technology humanist: someone who could understand technology not only as infrastructure, but as a multifactor phenomenon, which impacts culture, economy, communication, and human behavior.

But there was always a limitation.

Whenever I wanted to move from thinking to doing — from strategy to interface, from concept to prototype, from idea to system — I needed someone else to execute. A designer, a developer, an editor, a technician.

That dependency created friction.

Not because technical work does not matter. It matters enormously. But in many projects, the final decision-making power ended up in the hands of the people who knew how to build, even when they did not necessarily have the broader vision of what should be built, why it mattered, or how it should work for real people.

Generative AI changed that equation.

At first, it was overwhelming. It seemed like I had to absorb tasks that used to belong to other professionals. But as the tools improved, something shifted. I started learning faster. I started testing faster. I started building faster.

The distance between thinking and making became shorter.

That is the foundation behind CatchDog.

With an AI-driven mindset, I can now create not only content — text, images, video, scripts, explainers — but also functional systems: websites, dashboards, automations, lightweight apps, prototypes, and internal tools that actually work.

This does not mean that expertise disappears. It means that the center of gravity changes.

In many cases, generative AI lowers the barrier to execution. That can produce mediocre work when there is no strong judgment behind it. But for someone with years of experience analyzing technology, business, communication, and human behavior, it creates the opposite effect: it unlocks execution.

It allows the person with the vision to build.

That is why this moment feels liberating to me. Coming from journalism and the humanities is a huge advantage. It means I do not approach AI as a toy, a trend, a prompt trick, or just a complex tool. I approach it as a system of social, economic, and operational transformation. I have the main frame of it.

CatchDog exists because I no longer have to stop at analysis.

I can think, design, test, build, and deliver. 

And for small and mid-sized businesses, that matters. They do not always need a massive software project. They need someone who can understand the real problem, translate it into a practical digital solution, and build something useful without turning the process into an expensive, overcomplicated implementation.

That is the kind of work I want CatchDog to do.

Not technology for its own sake.

Not AI as decoration.

Technology shaped by judgment, strategy, and human understanding — and finally built by the same kind of mind that knows why it should exist.

title: Technology in — and with More — Democracy
excerpt: Argentina’s President Javier Milei proposes granting special legal status to AI-run companies and DAOs, allowing them to operate under limited-liability structures. But giving non-human entities greater autonomy without clear human accountability could deepen economic concentration and create serious risks for Argentine democracy.
body:
“Today, DAOs — Decentralized Autonomous Organizations operating on blockchain — are plutocracies.” It was not the only forceful statement Primavera De Filippi gave me during our interview, but it is a good starting point.

De Filippi, a lawyer and academic working at Harvard, is one of the most recognized researchers in the relationship between law and technology. I interviewed her in November 2025, during the launch of Indonesia’s official blockchain. Distancing herself from the optimism prevailing in Bali, she argued that technology without regulation is useless, dangerous, or both.

We learned something similar during the first stages of artificial intelligence. In 2016, *State v. Loomis* raised a central problem: if software created by a company cannot be fully explained by its programmers — meaning that no human being can be held responsible for its operation — then its conclusions cannot be accepted by society as expressions of truth.

In other words, there is no freedom without responsibility. This is why algorithmic governance has become one of the central issues of democracy.

In the Western world, freedom is administered through a complex mechanism that balances capitalism and democracy. Until recently, law schools taught *United States v. AT&T* as one of the clearest expressions of that balance. In 1982, in the country that prioritizes economic growth and capital creation above almost everything else, the courts ordered a telecommunications company to be divided into seven parts because it had abused its dominant position and become a monopoly.

Despite that precedent, Big Tech companies are now the dominant actors in communication — understood broadly as every form of symbolic exchange — and their abuse of market power is well documented.

Google was found in the United States to have illegally maintained a monopoly in search and related advertising. In Europe, it was sanctioned for favoring Google Shopping, imposing conditions on Android manufacturers and restricting competition through AdSense. The FTC accused Meta of maintaining its monopoly in personal social networks through a strategy of buying or burying competitors, especially Instagram and WhatsApp. Microsoft faced proceedings in Europe and the United States over the way it imposed products after the installation of Windows.

In generative AI, the business is also concentrated in very few hands. Big Tech companies participate simultaneously as investors, customers and suppliers.

Anthropic is a clear example. Amazon and Alphabet invest billions in the laboratory, while Anthropic commits even larger amounts to purchasing computing capacity from them. Amazon agreed to invest up to $25 billion, while Anthropic committed to spending more than $100 billion on AWS over ten years. At the same time, Alphabet agreed to invest up to $40 billion, while Anthropic reportedly assumed commitments worth $200 billion with Google Cloud and its chips.

Anthropic and OpenAI plan to go public, while their valuations are expected to increase dramatically. Like Gemini and the other major players, they follow the same adoption strategy: extraordinary technological disruption sustained by private capital willing to absorb enormous losses until a company captures the market. The model is known as “winner takes all.”

Once these companies become so large that legislation cannot stop them and fines no longer hurt them, they begin recovering the money invested. They raise subscription prices, capture data and partner with governments.

That is what Big Tech did.

## Non-human entities legally recognized in the United States

Before continuing, it is necessary to distinguish DAOs from AI systems. DAOs are considered non-human entities because their contracts execute automatically on Blockchain without human intervention. AI, meanwhile, refers to computer systems capable of learning and making decisions without human intervention, whether or not they operate on blockchain.

In this context, would democracy benefit from a State granting legal personality to non-human entities?

Let us return to responsibility.

In his *Financial Times* article, Argentine President Javier Milei uses the creation of limited liability companies as the precedent for his proposal. In Argentina, the equivalent structures are the SRL and the SA.

Creating a legal entity as an economic subject allows liability before the courts to be patrimonial: the company responds with its own assets. But when those assets are insufficient to compensate for damages, the law normally allows the identification of the human beings responsible for the decisions, so that their personal assets may also be reached.

With DAOs, identifying who decides and how decisions are made is extremely complex, especially because one of blockchain’s most valued characteristics is anonymity.

Nevertheless, De Filippi co-authored a regulatory model adopted in Utah in 2024, and later in Wyoming and Tennessee. Under those frameworks, DAOs receive legal personality, but they are also subject to specific conditions:

* They can be sued.
* They must have identifiable assets.
* They must have at least one human legal representative.
* Limited liability does not apply in cases involving personal wrongdoing, bad faith or refusal to obey a court order.

Because blockchain operations can be audited and their code is exposed, these jurisdictions consider that transparency partly compensates for the risk that a DAO may become undercapitalized. Even so, if no member personally committed an unlawful act or voted against compliance with a judgment, the injured party may remain uncompensated.

The risk is similar to the one created by traditional corporations, but it is aggravated because DAOs may have no board of directors, and being a beneficiary or token holder does not automatically make someone legally responsible.

At the same time, the United States government recently urged Anthropic to prevent foreign nationals from accessing its two new AI models, Mythos and Fable, because it considered them a threat to national security.

The Trump administration and Anthropic have also been involved in a legal dispute since the company refused to provide its AI for certain military and domestic cyber-surveillance purposes.

The best analysts agree that losing control over AI is a real risk. Anthropic itself has repeatedly called for a system of joint supervision between governments and private companies.

In one of its latest blog posts, the company argued that if AI achieves even part of its potential, the world may experience unprecedented abundance, and the economic challenge will no longer be how to generate growth but how to distribute it.

Anthropic has announced investments in research intended to preserve employment and has proposed regulatory frameworks both for AI and for the economic policies that will be needed in this scenario. It reasons that AI is advancing exponentially, while bureaucratic procedures were designed for a slower world.

The company also stresses that governments must be able to demand transparency from developers and prevent products from entering the market without proper prior controls.

It follows that deregulating technological progress does not appear to benefit society as a whole.

Even the president of the United States, who initially argued that government should not interfere with technological innovation, is now using the powers of his office to halt an advance he considers dangerous to the country he governs.

Anthropic’s proposal for shared AI governance is not the only one. But it clearly shows that if technology is expected to benefit society, democratic institutions and the law must play a central role.

In the *Financial Times*, Milei argues that AI should not be regulated. He then announces a legal framework that would incorporate entities managed by robots or AI through a reform of corporate law, together with a “competitive tax environment.” The objective is clearly to attract foreign investment.

Two conclusions follow from this analysis.

First, the experiences of Utah, Wyoming and Tennessee — together with failed initiatives in Estonia and Europe — provide no reason to believe that offering the framework proposed by Milei would necessarily benefit Argentina.

The risks are significant, and identifying responsible parties may become almost impossible. The flow of cryptocurrency funds is opaque, while the knowledge economy does not generate enough employment to transform Argentina’s economic structure. Argentina is also expensive compared with India, Pakistan or the Philippines, where software companies increasingly hire remote workers.

As Anthropic itself recognizes, the current challenge is how to distribute wealth created with fewer human workers. So far, that wealth flows mainly toward a small number of extraordinarily powerful corporations.

Second, democracy — understood as a system of political and social organization intended to correct the imbalances produced by capitalism — always requires strong rules and institutions.

The courts operate as the balancing point of that system. But without responsible human beings — and the ultimate beneficiaries of artificial corporations are not necessarily legally responsible — the courts may have no one to pursue.

De Filippi argues that “law is the articulator of democracy, and when we discuss new technologies, it needs clear pressure points to guarantee governance.”

The most solid and prestigious Spanish-speaking institution working on AI regulation is the University of Buenos Aires’ Innovation and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, UBA IALAB.

In *Artificial Intelligence Agents and Agentic Workflows*, published one year ago, the laboratory anticipated the level of automation we now see and argued that, depending on social risk and impact, artificial entities must adopt a Human-in-the-Loop model. Human beings must actively participate in the decision-making processes of artificial systems.

The same concept appears in *Centaur Organizations*, published in September 2025. Although the new era of information-processing organizations requires far fewer employees, humans must remain the curators, designers, directors and strategic auditors of autonomous systems.

Plutocracy — the word used by De Filippi at the beginning of this article — means government by the wealthy.

Blockchain attempted to rebuild the internet as a space of absolute freedom, without government. The result is that many DAOs are now controlled by those who own the largest number of tokens — in other words, by those who possess the most crypto wealth.

In unequal countries such as Argentina, democracy is the final refuge of those with the least economic power against those who possess the most. Without rules and without human beings who can be held accountable, warning lights appear everywhere.

It is not reasonable for non-human entities to gain autonomy without control. It is even less reasonable for money to receive a legal domicile without truly responsible human actors behind it.

Democracy weakens when freedom exists without responsibility.
